Two tutorials in one page: Skin & soft-tissue tumors and Wound healing. Both use the slides (black) and the doctor's notes (green). Everything the gifts asked is in red.

Part A — Skin & soft-tissue lesions

The big picture

  • Skin is built from epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous fat, arteries, veins, hair follicles and nerves — a tumor can arise from any of these components. Skin tumors divide broadly into benign vs malignant.
  • Tumor = a mass / neoplasm. It does not necessarily mean cancer.
  • Slides outline: types of tumors (benign, malignant) · benign tumors (hematoma, abscess, lipoma, sebaceous cyst) · skin cancers (SCC, BCC, melanoma) · vascular lesions.
Benign (4 common)Malignant (3 major)Vascular (2 groups)
Hematoma (blood)Basal cell carcinoma (BCC)Hemangioma
Lipoma (fat)Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)Vascular malformation
Sebaceous cyst (sebum)Malignant melanomaBoth benign; told apart by natural history
Abscess (pus)

Common benign lesions

HematomaLipomaSebaceous cystAbscess
What it isBlood collection beneath skinBenign tumor of fatBlocked gland opening → sebum accumulatesLocalized infection / pus
CourseAfter trauma (minor trauma if anticoagulated)Chronic, slow-growingChronic/dormant; may become inflamedAcute
SymptomsBruising, or swelling that may expand; ± compressionPainless (spontaneous pain = worry)Painless unless inflamed/infectedVery painful, tender, erythema ± fever
Exam clueDiscoloration / expanding swellingMobile, soft-firm, compressiblePunctum; firmer; thick chalky sebumErythema ± ulceration/discharge
ImagingUS or MRI (X-ray poor)US or MRIClinical ± USUS ± MRI
ManagementObserve if stable; drain if expanding/compressingObserve; excise if concerning or cosmeticInflamed: antibiotics → excise later; else exciseI&D + antibiotics; pack, leave open

Hematoma

  • Result of traumatic injury to the skin or the tissues beneath; damaged vessels leak, blood pools → bruise; as it clots → swelling and pain.
  • Usually no treatment needed — cold sponging and analgesics relieve pain and swelling.
  • Normal patient: usually needs significant trauma. Anticoagulated patient: minor trauma may cause a significant hematoma.
  • Presentation: bruising/discoloration only, or a swelling that may enlarge. A flat/stable hematoma usually causes no compression; an expanding one can compress an artery (pallor, ↓ distal O₂ saturation) or a nerve (numbness ± weakness).
  • Imaging: US or MRI — X-ray does not show it well. In general MRI is better for soft tissue, CT for bone.
  • Observe a stable, non-expanding, non-compressive hematoma (warm compress, elevate a limb). Drain/evacuate (small incision) if it is expanding, compressing an artery/nerve, or threatening the overlying skin.
  • Swelling, skin discoloration and clots oozing from the wound after restarting anticoagulation → hematoma (printed "hamartoma" in the source). 441

Lipoma

Lipomas

  • History: chronic swelling, painless (rarely painful). Exam: anywhere, no skin change, mobile, firm. Investigation: US or CT if needed. Management: rarely biopsied; usually encapsulated; 99.9% benign — removed for cosmetic reasons.
  • Most common benign soft-tissue tumor. Chronic, slow-growing, painless; anywhere (back, head); size may change with body weight.
  • Pain is uncommon (pressure on bone/nerve). Red flag: spontaneous pain is more concerning for malignancy.
  • Exam: normal overlying skin, mobile side to side, soft but somewhat firm (capsule), more compressible than a sebaceous cyst. US or MRI if needed.
  • Most → observation. Excise if the diagnosis is concerning or the patient wants it removed. Counsel: removal replaces the lump with a scar.

Sebaceous cyst

Sebaceous cysts and the steps of excision (punctum, elliptical incision, removal of the cyst, closure)

  • History: chronic swelling (acute → infected?), painless (painful → infected?). Exam: usually on the head, has a punctum; painful, inflamed and discharging if infected. Investigation: US but usually clinical. Management: infected → antibiotics, then excision; not infected → can be excised.
  • Obstruction of the sebaceous gland opening → sebum accumulates. Common on the head/neck and hair-bearing areas.
  • High-yield picture/MCQ finding: punctum — the small dot over the lesion. See a punctum, think sebaceous cyst.
  • Non-inflamed it resembles a lipoma (painless); inflamed/infected it resembles an abscess (painful).
  • Inflamed/infected → antibiotics first → inflammation settles → excise later. Non-infected → excise. Don't excise during acute inflammation — the wall becomes fragile and is hard to remove completely.

Abscess

  • History: acute painful swelling, erythema ± fever (sepsis). Exam: tender, erythema, discharge. Investigation: US but usually clinical. Management: incision and drainage + antibiotics (keep open and pack).
  • Acute, very painful swelling ± fever; tenderness + erythema ± leukocytosis; may ulcerate/discharge. US ± MRI when needed.
  • Incision & drainage + antibiotics → pack the wound and leave it open. Never close an abscess primarily — residual pus may remain; leaving it open allows continued drainage.
  • Hidradenitis suppurativa is a disease of the apocrine sweat glands (axilla, groin). 427 ×2

Malignant skin tumors

  • Three major types differing mostly in aggressiveness: BCC (least aggressive, essentially no metastasis) → SCC (more aggressive, faster) → melanoma (most aggressive).

Identifying skin cancer · basal cell vs squamous cell carcinoma

  • Shared risk factors for BCC & SCC (ask about each): sun exposure (occupation — the major risk factor), childhood/recurrent sunburn, light skin, immunosuppression/immunosuppressive drugs.
Basal cell carcinomaSquamous cell carcinoma
Most common inOtherwise normal patientsImmunocompromised / transplant patients
Typical sitesNose, eyelidsEar, around the lips
GrowthSlow; often present for yearsFaster, more aggressive
AppearanceInnocuous; recurrent small scab; may ulcerateMore destructive; looks abnormal earlier
MetastasisVery low potentialMore than BCC
Excision margin (lecture)0.5–1 cm1–2 cm
Extra optionsCryotherapy if surgery not toleratedRadiotherapy as additional treatment
Rule of thumb: normal patient → BCC is the most common skin cancer. Immunocompromised/transplant patient → SCC is the most common.
  • Picture of an elderly face with a crusted, ulcerated nodule on the cheek → keyed squamous cell carcinoma. 435
  • Rodent ulcer = basal cell carcinoma. 426
  • Elderly man, scaly erythematous lesion with irregular borders on the sun-exposed dorsum of the forearm → actinic keratosis (pre-malignant → SCC). 436 Final

Diagnosis — biopsy

  • Slides: biopsy types — punch, incisional, excisional.
TypeWhat it doesUsed forKey pro / con
PunchPen-like punch removes a 2–3 mm cylinder of skinSimple, minor procedureSamples a small % → may not represent the lesion
IncisionalRemoves part of the lesion, full thicknessLarge lesionsPartial sample may not represent the tumor
ExcisionalRemoves the entire lesion with a small margin (~2 mm)Small lesions (e.g. small BCC)Diagnosis + possible definitive treatment in one step
FNAFine-needle aspirationDeeper structuresNot usual for superficial skin lesions

Treatment — excision with margins

  • Slides: Mohs micrographic surgery · surgical excision with margins · destructive treatment (cryosurgery, curettage and electrodesiccation, photodynamic therapy) · radiotherapy (SCC).
  • Main treatment of BCC, SCC and melanoma = surgical excision with margins; the more aggressive the tumor, the wider the margin: BCC 0.5–1 cm · SCC 1–2 cm · melanoma 2–4 cm (lecture figures).
  • The margin is added on both sides: a 1-cm lesion with 1-cm margins needs an excision ~3 cm wide.
  • Mohs micrographic surgery: for sites where wide margins would cause major loss (eyelid, nose). Remove tumor → map margins → examine histologically → re-excise only where positive, repeat. Very accurate, spares normal tissue; but time-consuming (~4–5 h) and needs a specialized center.
  • Cryotherapy/destructive treatment if the patient can't tolerate surgery; radiotherapy as additional treatment, particularly for SCC.

Malignant melanoma

  • Evaluated as a pigmented lesion — key differential benign nevus vs melanoma. The most aggressive skin cancer.
ABCDEFavors benignConcerning for melanoma
AsymmetrySymmetricAsymmetric
BorderSmooth, regularIrregular / ill-defined
ColorUniformMultiple shades
DiameterSmaller> 6 mm (¼ inch)
EvolutionStable for yearsChange in size or appearance
  • Don't be reassured by size alone — even a small suspicious pigmented lesion should be assessed.
  • Prognosis depends on depth: < 1 mm → ~100% 5-year survival; > 4 mm → ~50%.
  • Treatment: excision with the widest margins (2–4 cm in the lecture's comparison).
  • Most common type of melanoma → superficial spreading melanoma. 429 ×4

Vascular skin lesions

  • Hemangioma vs vascular malformations: high-flow, and low-flow (venous, capillary, lymphatic).

Hemangioma · port-wine stain (capillary malformation)

At birthEarly lifeFollowing years
HemangiomaAbsent or barely visibleRapid proliferation in the first year, out of proportion to growthGradual involution
Vascular malformationPresentGrows proportionally with the childPersists, no involution
  • Both are generally benign; treatment is often driven mainly by cosmetic considerations.

Part B — Wound healing

Definitions

  • Wound: disruption of normal anatomical structure and function.
  • Acute wound: proceeds through an orderly, timely repair that restores function and anatomy (3–4 weeks).
  • Chronic wound: repair without a sustained anatomic and functional result (beyond 6 weeks).
  • Healing: the organism's response to a physical disruption, to repair the defect.
  • Abnormal healing: overgrowth (keloid, hypertrophic scar), undergrowth (wide, thin or chronic unstable scar), abnormal pigmentation (hypo/hyper).
  • Scar formation: substitution of a different matrix as a patch to immediately re-establish physical and physiological continuity. Regeneration: recreating the original organ by the developmental process that created it.

Phases of normal wound healing

  • 1 Hemostasis → 2 Inflammatory → 3 Proliferative → 4 Remodeling. Wound contraction occurs throughout, starting from the proliferative phase.
PhaseDuration (slides)Time unitMain cellMain job
Hemostasis5–10 minMinutesPlateletsStop bleeding → platelet plug
Inflammation1–4 daysDaysNeutrophils → macrophagesClean / debride, kill bacteria
ProliferationDay 3 → 3 weeksWeeksFibroblastsCollagen synthesis
Remodeling3 weeks → 1 yearMonths → 1 yearFibroblastsCollagen reorganisation (III → I)
  • Exams test the time unit (minutes vs days vs weeks vs months/year), not 3 vs 5 days.
  • The longest phase of wound healing → remodelling. 438 Final

Hemostasis

  • Vasoconstriction → platelet plug → intrinsic and extrinsic pathways.
  • Platelets release PDGF, TGF-β, FGF → chemotaxis, fibrogenesis, angiogenesis.
  • Impaired by aspirin, warfarin, bleeding disorders — antiplatelets mainly hit the hemostatic phase.

Inflammatory (migratory) phase

  • Rubor, tumor, calor, dolor. PMNs within 6–8 h, for 48–72 h. Monocytes peak at 24–36 h → mature into macrophages.
  • Goal: clean/debride the wound and eliminate bacteria before collagen is laid down. Impaired by diabetes, immunosuppression, steroids, chemotherapy, HIV.

Macrophage roles (phagocytosis, matrix synthesis, angiogenesis) · the inflammatory phase

Proliferative (fibroplasia) phase

  • Starts day 2–3; fibroblasts peak at 7–14 days; collagen synthesis for 3–6 weeks; lasts 2–4 weeks.
  • Protect the wound: infection or repeated injury in the first month → poorer scar; avoid excessive strain across the wound for ~1–1.5 months.

Remodeling phase

  • Starts at 3 weeks; collagen synthesis peaks at 3 weeks then synthesis = degradation; fibres reorganise.
  • Collagen III replaced by I → normal 4:1 (I:III). May take up to 1 year. Tensile strength 80% of pre-injury at 60 days.
  • The scar keeps changing for up to 1 year → assess the final scar at ~1 year and avoid definitive scar revision before ~1 year.

Collagen

  • 90% type I. Normal I:III = 4:1; hypertrophic scar 2:1.
  • Formation inhibited by: colchicine, penicillamine, steroids, vitamin C deficiency, iron deficiency.
  • Wording trap: most common collagen in normal skin = type I; in a hypertrophic scar = still type I; the collagen in relative excess in a hypertrophic scar = type III.

Epithelial repair & contraction

  • Epithelial continuity is re-established by mobilization, migration, mitosis and cellular differentiation.
  • Wound contraction is an active, normal, essential part of healing; its rate depends on the number of myofibroblasts (fibroblast-like cells with smooth-muscle actin).
  • Contracture = the undesirable result of excessive contraction and fibrosis.
  • High-risk sites: wounds across joints and around orifices (mouth, nose, ear, perianal) need better coverage to minimize contracture.
  • Burn-scar contracture release at the elbow: the reconstruction most likely to re-contract → split-thickness skin graft (thin grafts contract most; flaps contract least). 435 ×3

Factors affecting healing

  • Local: infection, radiation, blood supply, nerve supply, trauma, hydration, temperature.
  • Systemic — congenital: pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Ehlers–Danlos (defective collagen synthesis/cross-linking), cutis laxa, progeria, Werner syndrome, epidermolysis bullosa.
  • Systemic — acquired: nutrition, drugs, endocrine, age, smoking.
FactorEffect (slides)
Vitamin ADeficiency delays healing; 25,000 IU PO daily ↑ tensile strength; 200,000 IU topical q8h ↑ epithelialization
Vitamin CNeeded for collagen synthesis; scurvy → immature fibroblasts, deficient collagen, capillary haemorrhage, ↓ tensile strength
Vitamin EAntioxidant, membrane stabiliser; large doses may inhibit healing; unproven to reduce scarring
ZincEnzyme cofactor; deficiency impairs epithelial and fibroblast proliferation
Steroids↓ inflammation and subsequent healing
NSAIDs↓ collagen synthesis, inhibit platelet aggregation
Antineoplastics↓ fibroblast proliferation and contraction; few/no problems if given 10–14 days after closure
DiabetesDelayed healing — neuropathy rather than small-vessel disease may be responsible
AgeAll stages protracted; healed wounds weaker
SmokingNicotine → vasoconstriction; CO shifts the O₂ curve → ↓ tissue oxygenation
Infection> 10⁵ organisms per gram of tissue = infected, unlikely to heal without treatment
RadiationEndothelial/capillary damage; fibroblasts make less collagen; lymphatics destroyed → oedema, infection
Blood supply↓ perfusion → ↓ oxygenation; fibroblasts are O₂-sensitive → ↓ collagen, matrix, angiogenesis, epithelialization
  • Doctor's timing rule: separate radiation and surgery by ~3 weeks and chemotherapy and surgery by ~2 weeks (either side) when clinically possible.
  • Diabetes impairs healing two ways: neutrophil dysfunction (infection) + neuropathy (repeated unnoticed trauma). Smoking acts through perfusion.
  • Chemotherapy after an oncologic resection — the gift key is 3 weeks (slides: 10–14 days; doctor: ~2 weeks). Answer 3 weeks in this question. 438 ×6
  • Multivitamins in a well-nourished patient → no effect on healing. 437 Final ×2
  • Elective plastic surgery: the history item that affects the result → smoking. 437 Final
  • Infected, opened and dressed wound → prolonged proliferative phase 432 Final ×3; huge infected necrotic sacral ulcer in a bed-bound diabetic → inflammatory and proliferative phases both increased. 429 Final

Types of wound healing

  • Primary intention: primary closure → least scarring.
  • Secondary intention: heals by granulation, contraction and epithelialization.
  • Tertiary intention (delayed primary closure): for contaminated wounds.

Primary closure (sutured wound) · healing by secondary intention (open wound)

PrimaryTertiary (delayed primary)Secondary
HowCleaned and closed at onceLeft open, cleaned/debrided, closed laterGranulation + contraction, never closed
WhenFresh wound within ~6 h (up to 12–18 h if well cleaned)Late or dirty woundsLarge/dirty wounds; patient unfit for surgery
ClosureImmediate~3–4 days once contamination controlledNever surgically
Speed & scarFastest, bestIntermediateSlowest, worst
  • Ranking for speed and scar quality: primary > tertiary > secondary. Secondary wins only on least intervention.
  • Clean 2 × 0.5 cm forehead laceration after debridement → primary closure with appropriate tension. 436 Final
  • Single puncture wound after cleaning and debridement → don't close it; give oral antibiotics (puncture/bite wounds are never sutured). 436 Final

Abnormal scarring — keloid vs hypertrophic scar

KeloidHypertrophic scar
Wound borderOutgrows (extends beyond)Remains within
Family historySignificantLow
Race / sexDark > light skin; females > malesLow racial incidence; equal sex ratio
AgeMost common 10–30 yearsAny age
Onset & courseMonths (even years) after surgery; rarely subsidesSoon after surgery (1–3 months); subsides with time
SitesFace, earlobes, anterior chest, deltoidAcross flexor surfaces; tension closure
After excisionHigh recurrenceBetter outcome

Earlobe keloids · hypertrophic scar

  • The main difference: keloids extend beyond the original zone of injury. 429 ×3
  • Earlobe swelling 2 months after piercing in a dark-skinned woman → keloid 438 Final; a scar within the piercing at 4 weeks → hypertrophic scar (keyed). 437 Final
  • Keloid after sternotomy → expect itching (keyed A; one version also marked D, size fluctuation). 439 Final

Treatment

  • Prevention — avoid: unnecessary surgery, high-risk patients/sites, closure under tension, crossing joint lines, rough tissue handling, infection and hematoma.
  • Therapeutic: pressure garments, silicone sheets, steroid injections, radiation, revision.
  • Least → most invasive: pressure → silicone → intralesional steroid → revision (both scars) → radiation (keloid only, especially recurrent keloid after re-excision, possibly a single dose).
  • Mild hypertrophic scar 4 weeks after closure → first line silicone sheeting + compression garments. 436 Final ×2

Part C — Wound care, sutures & reconstruction (from past exams)

  • Skin closure after excising a superficial forearm lipoma → 4-0 Monocryl, cutting needle, subcuticular (skin needs a cutting needle; fine absorbable monofilament for subcuticular). 438 ×6
  • Face sutures come out early (3–5 days): forehead laceration with 5-0 Prolene → remove at 4 days (keyed). 438 ×3
  • Post-op wound swellings: soft fluctuant, no erythema → seroma 442; serosanguinous discharge on pressure with intact skin sutures → partial (fascial) dehiscence. 439
  • Diabetic foot ulcer (1 × 2 cm, foot pain): wound care is the base; revascularization is the most important step when there is ischaemia (source keys vary A/B/C/D) 439 Final ×6; "besides wound care" → revascularization. 439 Final
  • 10 × 10 cm sacral pressure sore with a healthy granulating bed in a paraplegic → dressing changes, then surgical (flap) closure. 437 Final ×6
  • Reconstructive ladder: bottom/first rung = primary closure 427 ×2 → secondary intention → skin graft → local flap → distant flap → top = free flap. 428 Final
  • Not enough donor skin for a 35% third-degree burn → meshing the split-thickness graft (expands it to cover more area). 438 ×7
